summary.text: The central limit theorem says that, under appropriate conditions, the distribution of a normalized sample mean converges to a standard normal distribution.
This holds even when the original variables are not themselves normally distributed.
That makes it key, because methods that work for normal distributions can then apply to many problems involving other distributions.

facts.label: Earliest version
facts.value: Normal approximation to the binomial, the de Moivre-Laplace theorem

facts.label: Link to large numbers
facts.value: The averages head to a limit, and this describes their fluctuations

items.prompt: Many people each take a large sample and compute its average. If all those averages are collected, what shape should their distribution have?

options.label: A flat line across all values
Whatever shape the raw data had
Two separate peaks
Close to a normal distribution

items.explain: If the sample size is large enough, the probability distribution of these averages will closely approximate a normal distribution.

items.prompt: The individual measurements are skewed and nothing like a bell shape. Can the theorem still say something about their averages?

options.label: Yes, since it holds even without normal originals
No, the originals must be normal first
No, averages cannot be studied at all
Yes, but only for a single measurement

items.explain: The theorem holds even if the original variables themselves are not normally distributed.

items.prompt: The law of large numbers says a sample average heads toward the true mean. What does the central limit theorem add?

options.label: It proves the average never moves at all
It replaces the true mean with zero
It describes how the average fluctuates around that mean
It says the average is always exactly right

items.explain: The classical theorem describes the size and the distributional form of the fluctuations around the deterministic number during this convergence.

items.prompt: The usual form needs observations that are independent and identically distributed. Must that always hold?

options.label: Yes, with no exceptions
Yes, since any change ruins normality
No, the theorem only needs one observation
No, it can be weakened under certain conditions

items.explain: The requirement can be weakened: convergence to the normal distribution also occurs for non-identical distributions or non-independent observations if they meet certain conditions.

items.prompt: The earliest version of the idea used the normal curve to approximate which other distribution?

options.label: The Cauchy distribution
The binomial distribution
The Pareto distribution
The uniform distribution

items.explain: The earliest version, the de Moivre-Laplace theorem, says the normal distribution may be used as an approximation to the binomial distribution.

items.prompt: Why is this theorem so valuable to statisticians working with non-normal data?

options.label: It turns every data set into a normal one
It makes sampling unnecessary
It removes all random variation
Methods built for normal distributions can serve other problems

items.explain: It implies that methods that work for normal distributions can be applicable to many problems involving other types of distributions.
